papers.title: Calcified choroid plexus papilloma of the temporal horn presenting with seizures in an adult without hydrocephalus: An illustrative case.
papers.abstract: Choroid plexus papillomas (CPPs) are rare, benign tumors that typically occur in pediatric patients and result in hydrocephalus. Presentations in an adult featuring seizures, particularly focal impaired awareness seizures, occur infrequently, especially in the absence of hydrocephalus. A 50-year-old female exhibited episodes of temporary unresponsiveness characteristic of a focal impaired awareness seizure. Imaging identified a calcified mesial temporal lesion; electroencephalogram revealed epileptiform discharges. Surgical pathology confirmed the presence of CPP. The patient began treatment with levetiracetam and later underwent surgical removal of the tumor. Postoperatively, the patient experienced no seizures and exhibited no neurological deficits. While CPPs usually cause hydrocephalus, this case had no ventricular enlargement on imaging. Instead, a calcified CPP diagnostically mimicked a cavernoma by presenting solely with seizures and a calcified intraventricular temporal-horn mass in a 50-year-old adult; typically, CPPs present in the fourth ventricle rather than the temporal horn, whereas cavernomas regularly present in the temporal lobe with a classically "popcorn-like" appearance. Thus, CPPs can cause focal seizures via local cortical irritation that is calcified, similarly to a cavernoma; CPPs can also present in a middle-aged adult rather than a pediatric patient and lack the most common diagnostic sign of hydrocephalus. The cumulative rarity of a CPP that lacks hydrocephalus, causes seizures, contains calcifications, and manifests later in life makes for an incredibly atypical and unique case of CPP. Without pathology, the given symptoms and imaging were more suggestive of a cavernous malformation rather than a CPP, highlighting the importance of biopsy for an accurate diagnosis; early surgical resection is crucial and may be curative.

papers.title: Relationship of dental malocclusions with development of bruxism in adults.
papers.abstract: This study assessed the relationship of dental malocclusions with the development of bruxism in adults between 18 and 25 years. This cross-sectional study evaluated 564 patients including 324 patients with dental malocclusions comprising the test group and 240 patients without dental malocclusion comprising the control group. The type and severity of malocclusions were determined by an orthodontist. All patients were between 18 and 25 years. A questionnaire was used to assess the presence/absence and severity of bruxism and confounding factors related to bruxism in the participants. Their psychological status was assessed by using the Symptom Checklist-25 (SCL-25). Data were analyzed using Mann-Whitney test, Chi-square test, and logistic regression (alpha = 0.05). The prevalence of bruxism was 29.6%; this rate was 27.3% for daily bruxism (DB) and 9.6% for sleep bruxism (SB). The malocclusion group had significantly higher prevalence of bruxism in general, DB, and SB (P = 0.001). Each 1-year increase in age decreased the odds of bruxism by 16%. The odds of bruxism in patients with chipped incisal edges and sleep disorder were 9.01 and 3.11 times higher than those in other individuals, respectively. Each one-unit increase in the SCL-25 score increased the odds of bruxism by 5%. Bruxism had a significantly higher prevalence in those with chipped incisal edges and those with hypertrophy of the muscles of mastication (P < 0.05). Malocclusion was associated with significantly higher prevalence of bruxism. Age, psychological symptoms, and intake of some antidepressants were also found to play a role in increasing the risk of bruxism.

papers.title: Intraoperative electroencephalography burst suppression during endoscopic third ventriculostomy: Case report and implications for neuromonitoring.
papers.abstract: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) is a common treatment for obstructive hydrocephalus. Intraoperative hemodynamic disturbances are well recognized. Their concurrent association with cortical suppression on electroencephalography (EEG), particularly burst suppression, has rarely been reported, and intraoperative EEG is seldom used during ETV. A 28-year-old woman underwent ETV for obstructive hydrocephalus secondary to a tectal glioma. Shortly after endoscope insertion and ventricular irrigation, she developed two successive episodes of severe tachycardia and an acute hypertensive crisis, each coinciding with an abrupt bilateral fall in fronto-temporal electrocortical activity with burst suppression on two-channel processed EEG. Irrigation was stopped and the endoscope was withdrawn. Systemic hemodynamics normalized within 15 min, whereas the EEG required 55 min to recover. The patient recovered to near-baseline within 4 h. This report represents only the second published case coupling an acute intraoperative hemodynamic surge with bilateral EEG burst suppression during ETV. Processed intraoperative EEG may be an additional early sign of an acute disturbance of cerebral function. Its added value remains unproven, since a hemodynamic emergency already mandates cessation of irrigation and endoscope withdrawal. Prospective evaluation with finer temporal sampling and raw-EEG recording is warranted.

papers.title: A Case of SLE Flare With Class IV Lupus Nephritis and Tuberculous Meningitis Presenting as Neuropsychiatric Symptoms: A Diagnostic Dilemma.
papers.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disease with potential neuropsychiatric involvement (NPSLE) and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections like tuberculosis (TB), particularly in endemic regions such as Nepal where the estimated incidence is 229 per 100,000 population. Differentiating NPSLE from tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is diagnostically challenging due to overlapping clinical and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings. A 25-year-old male with a 1-year history of SLE presented with facial puffiness, oral ulcers, polyarthritis, lower limb edema, and a 6-week history of renal symptoms. Laboratory investigations revealed microcytic anemia (Hb 7.4 g/dL), nephrotic-range proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 4.8 g/g), strongly positive anti-dsDNA, and low complement levels. ENA panel was positive for anti-Ro/SSA but negative for antiribosomal P and antiphospholipid antibodies. Renal biopsy confirmed class IV lupus nephritis (Activity Index 11/24 and Chronicity Index 3/12). Following intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy (500 mg/day for 3 days), he developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures and altered sensorium. EEG revealed epileptiform discharges. CSF analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (500 cells/μL and 80% lymphocytes), elevated protein (578 mg/dL), low glucose (1.4 mmol/L), and elevated ADA (10.9 U/L), suggestive of TBM despite negative GeneXpert MTB/RIF, viral PCR, and cryptococcal antigen assays. MRI brain showed cerebral atrophy, calcified granulomas in the right temporal lobe, and a nonspecific demyelinating white matter lesion. Based on clinical, CSF, and imaging findings, empirical antitubercular therapy (ATT) was initiated alongside tailored immunosuppression. The patient's neurological and renal status markedly improved with complete resolution of seizures. Distinguishing NPSLE from CNS infections requires careful evaluation of serial CSF parameters, biomarkers, and MRI findings. In endemic regions, empirical ATT should be initiated early when clinical and laboratory features suggest TBM, even when molecular or culture tests are negative. In SLE patients with neuropsychiatric symptoms in TB-endemic areas, clinicians must consider TBM even when definitive microbiological tests are negative. Early empirical treatment can significantly improve patient survival and long-term outcomes.

papers.title: Immunometabolic reprogramming: a working framework for disease development, endotype differentiation, and therapeutic considerations in pediatric asthma.
papers.abstract: Paediatric asthma exhibits marked clinical heterogeneity and cannot be simply considered the childhood counterpart of adult asthma. Early-life environmental exposures can reshape immune-cell metabolic programs and potentially drive long-lasting inflammatory phenotypes. Existing explanatory frameworks for paediatric asthma largely centre on Th2-related inflammation, epithelial-alarm signalling and neuro-immune crosstalk, while the contributions of immunometabolic processes to disease endotypes remain under-summarised. This review collates available evidence regarding metabolic reprogramming in the pathogenesis of paediatric asthma and provides an integrated immunometabolic perspective on this condition. Summarized evidence covers immunometabolic changes across key airway-resident and infiltrating cell populations. Discussion addresses core paediatric-specific biological features, including early-life developmental windows, virus-related trained immunity, obese asthma, circadian-sleep interactions, neuro-metabolic-immune communication and metabolomics-based endotyping. The framework is organized around substrate competition rather than a glycolysis-versus-OXPHOS binary, because Tregs, M2-like macrophages and pathogenic ILC2s share lipid and amino-acid pools but exert opposing functions. From these observations emerges a testable "Metabolic Latching Model" of how early-life insults establish persistent inflammatory memory through metabolism-epigenetic coupling, with "latching" operationally defined by exposure removal and persistence beyond responding-cell turnover. Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) and the Treg-to-effector balance are placed at the centre of this framework. Three hypotheses are prioritised as feasible with current technology: H1 (monocyte glycolytic baseline predicting wheeze-to-asthma transition), H4 (metabolic intervention in obese asthma), and H6 (the HDAC2-GSH/butyrate axis in steroid sensitivity). Current evidence suggests that immunometabolic reprogramming serves as one plausible contributing factor for the heterogeneity of paediatric asthma. This conceptual framework may bridge molecular metabolic findings and paediatric clinical contexts, and inform future mechanistic and clinical studies in this research area.

papers.title: Effects of Intensive Electroacupuncture on Nicotine Withdrawal and Withdrawal-Related Sleep Symptoms in Patients with Nicotine Dependence: A Three-Arm Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Whether intensive electroacupuncture (EA) during early nicotine withdrawal improves symptom trajectories remains unclear. To compare intensive EA with low-density EA and varenicline for withdrawal symptoms and explore withdrawal-related sleep symptoms. In this single-center, three-arm, open-label randomized trial, 114 participants were allocated equally to intensive EA, low-density EA, or varenicline for 4 weeks. EA was administered daily or every other day during week 1, respectively, and three times weekly during weeks 2-4. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, weeks 1-4, and 1 and 3 months after treatment. The main outcome for the present analysis was the week-1 change in Minnesota Nicotine Withdrawal Scale (MNWS) total score. Withdrawal-related sleep symptoms were assessed exploratorily using a score derived from two MNWS sleep-related items. Analyses used analysis of covariance and generalized estimating equations, with exploratory analyses of time-averaged symptom burden and post-treatment changes. Per-protocol analyses included 110 participants. At week 1, intensive EA was associated with lower adjusted MNWS scores than varenicline (mean difference, -5.75; 95% CI, -6.95 to -4.55) and low-density EA (-5.88; 95% CI, -7.08 to -4.67). Exploratory analyses suggested improvements in craving and withdrawal-related sleep symptoms. The proportions with exhaled carbon monoxide ≤4 ppm at 3 months after treatment were 29.7%, 18.9%, and 13.9% in the intensive EA, varenicline, and low-density EA groups, respectively (overall p=0.234). Intensive EA may alleviate withdrawal symptoms during early smoking cessation. Exploratory sleep findings require confirmation. The study did not establish a benefit for smoking abstinence, and longer follow-up is needed.

papers.title: Neural evidence for progressive decline of visual face recognition ability in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with deficits in recognizing familiar faces already at prodromal stages due to significant episodic and semantic memory impairment. However, whether the ability to visually discriminate and match unfamiliar faces for their identity also declines in AD remains unclear. We addressed this issue with a robust implicit electroencephalographic (EEG) measure of face identity recognition (FIR) relying on fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS). Thirty cognitively unimpaired (CU) individuals and thirty AD patients, including seventeen patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to AD and thirteen patients with dementia due to AD viewed stimulation sequences of the same unfamiliar face identity repeated at 6 Hz across size changes, with other identities appearing every 5 faces, eliciting a neural 1.2 Hz response indexing FIR. Stimuli were also presented upside down to control for low-level visual effects. While CU individuals exhibited robust FIR EEG responses at 1.2 Hz (and harmonics) over the occipito-temporal cortex, larger for upright than inverted faces, this response and the inversion effect were significantly reduced in patients with dementia due to AD but preserved in patients with MCI due to AD. These results indicate that unfamiliar FIR is preserved in patients at the prodromal stage, suggesting that familiar FIR difficulties previously observed during the prodromal phase of AD may stem from other cognitive factors, such as long-term memory impairments. In contrast, deficits in discriminating unfamiliar faces seem to emerge as the disease progresses. Overall, this study provides novel evidence for the processes underlying face identity recognition deficits in AD and highlights the diagnosticity of FPVS-EEG for assessing specific cognitive processes in neurodegenerative populations.

papers.title: ECAP-Guided Closed-Loop Spinal Cord Stimulation for Axial Thoracic Pain: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Thoracic spine pain is among the least commonly reported pain syndromes. Conventional therapeutic strategies are frequently ineffective and may be associated with adverse events. Closed-loop spinal cord stimulation (SCS) assisted with evoked compound action potentials (ECAPs) has emerged as a promising, safe and effective alternative. In this case report, we describe the successful use of ECAP-controlled closed-loop SCS in a patient with refractory thoracic spine pain. A female patient in her 40s presented with several axial thoracic pain refractory to all conservative and interventional therapies. Upon admission, the numeric rating scale (NRS) for pain score was 8/10. Functional limitations included restricted sleep duration (3 h) and limited standing and walking tolerance (20 min). The patient underwent a one-week trial of ECAP-controlled closed-loop SCS, during which 24 million smart adjustments were automatically performed to maintain consistent neural activation. The dose accuracy was ±5 μV, with a target ECAP of 19.4 μV, and the measure was 16.4 μV, and the patient used the device 100% of the time. Following treatment, the patient reported improvement in pain and functional outcomes, with NRS scores decreasing to 2/10, and substantial improvements in sleep (6 h), standing, and walking duration. This case suggests that ECAP-assisted closed-loop SCS may provide meaningful pain relief and functional improvements in patients with refractory spine pain.

papers.title: Case Report: Longitudinal evaluation of cerebrospinal fluid Alzheimer's disease core biomarkers in a case of refractory late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology.
papers.abstract: In recent years, late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology (LOEU) has increasingly been recognized as a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other forms of dementia. We present a case of refractory LOEU with progressive cognitive decline, longitudinally evaluated over more than 20 years using neuropsychological tests, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) AD core biomarkers (Aβ42/40 ratio, p-tau), electroencephalography, and neuroimaging. The CSF AD core biomarkers were consistently positive, indicating the presence of both amyloid and tau pathology; however, CSF Aβ levels markedly decreased in parallel with improved seizure control. Notably, the addition of low-dose perampanel (1 mg/day) led to improvement in both cognitive function and seizure control, while 18F-flutemetamol positron emission tomography remained visually negative despite exceeding the predefined quantitative Centiloid threshold. Two years later, seizure frequency increased again, cognitive function deteriorated, and amyloid PET became visually positive, accompanied by an increase in the quantitative Centiloid value. This longitudinal observation suggests that chronic epileptic activity may modify or confound the interpretation of CSF AD biomarker profiles and contribute to cognitive decline, while concomitant early or slowly progressive AD pathology cannot be excluded. The overall biomarker trajectory, including persistently positive CSF AD biomarkers and progressive amyloid PET findings, is compatible with evolving AD pathology, although the marked decline in absolute CSF Aβ concentrations during improved seizure control suggests that chronic epileptic activity may also influence biomarker dynamics. Careful interpretation of AD biomarkers is therefore essential in patients with LOEU, particularly in the era of anti-amyloid therapies.

papers.title: A multimodal optimisation framework for cardiac electrophysiology model personalisation using computed tomography and 12-lead electrocardiogram: Algorithm development and validation.
papers.abstract: Accurate parameterisation of cardiac patient-specific models is a major challenge. Here we aimed to test the feasibility of an optimised multimodal personalisation framework that combines structural information from computed tomography (CT) and 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) features, for high-fidelity simulations of ventricular tachycardia (VT). We studied a small cohort of six patients who had CT images and sinus-rhythm 12-lead ECGs available prior to VT ablation. The CT images were used to construct patient-specific biventricular simulation domains and to estimate ECG lead positions. We implemented a graphics processing unit-based computational pipeline and a two-stage optimisation framework consisting of: (i) an early activation onset estimation; and, (ii) the optimisation of conductivity parameter. For validation, the simulation outcomes were compared to clinical VT patterns and cycle lengths. Following early onset estimations, simulated 12-lead ECG signals achieved a 91.20 % mean Q wave, R wave, and S wave (QRS) peak accuracy. Using the optimised parameters, average QRS duration error was reduced to 3.94 ms, compared to 37.42 ms for baseline parameters. Notably, in four patients with available electro-anatomical VT maps, simulations reproduced the clinical VT patterns and cycle length closer to recordings than those obtained with baseline parameterisation. Our pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of a robust electrophysiology modelling framework able to perform multimodal personalisation by integrating sinus-rhythm ECGs and cardiac CT images for VT simulations with tractable computational time, paving the way for its clinical translation and a less invasive scar-related VT risk assessment.

papers.title: A Scoping Review of Deep Learning Methods for Photoplethysmography Data.
papers.abstract: Background: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a noninvasive optical sensing technique widely used to capture hemodynamic information, with broad deployment in both clinical monitoring systems and wearable devices. In recent years, the integration of deep learning has substantially advanced PPG signal analysis and expanded its applications across healthcare and nonhealthcare domains. Methods: We conducted a comprehensive literature search for studies applying deep learning to PPG data published between 2017 January 1 and 2025 December 31, using Google Scholar, PubMed, and Dimensions. The included studies were analyzed from 3 key perspectives: tasks, models, and data. Results: A total of 460 papers applying deep learning techniques to PPG signal analysis were included. These studies span a wide range of application domains, from traditional physiological monitoring tasks such as cardiovascular assessment to emerging applications including sleep analysis, cross-modality signal reconstruction, and biometric identification. Conclusions: Deep learning has substantially advanced PPG signal analysis by enabling more effective extraction of physiological information. Compared with traditional machine learning approaches reliant on handcrafted features, deep learning methods generally achieve improved performance and offer greater flexibility in model development. Nevertheless, several challenges remain, including limited availability of large-scale high-quality datasets, insufficient validation in real-world environments, and concerns over model interpretability, scalability, and computational efficiency. Addressing these challenges and exploring emerging research directions will be essential for further progress in deep learning-based PPG analysis.

papers.title: Between algorithmic alerts and bodily sensations: a qualitative study of post-PCI patients' experiences with wrist-worn heart health information.
papers.abstract: Smart wrist-worn devices are increasingly used by patients after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to monitor heart rate, rhythm-related alerts, sleep, activity, and other health-related data. However, limited qualitative evidence exists on how post-PCI patients interpret and respond to such information in daily life. This study aimed to explore how patients with coronary heart disease after PCI understand, evaluate, and respond to heart rate, heart rhythm, and health-related information generated by smart wrist-worn devices. A qualitative descriptive design was adopted. From January to May 2026, purposive sampling was used to recruit 23 post-PCI patients who had used smartwatches or smart bands in daily life. Semi-structured interviews were conducted, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Data collection and analysis were conducted concurrently until data saturation was achieved. Four themes were developed: (1) cardiac status became continuously datafied; (2) calibrating risk between alerts and sensations; (3) device information awaited medical interpretation; and (4) from self-management to disease burden. Patients did not simply accept or reject device-generated data. Instead, they interpreted alerts by comparing them with bodily sensations, previous cardiac events, stent implantation experiences, follow-up results, and healthcare professionals' explanations. Device information could enhance awareness of medication use, follow-up, and lifestyle management. However, when alerts lacked medical interpretation or follow-up response, they also increased uncertainty, worry, repeated self-monitoring, and perceived disease burden. Smart wrist-worn devices may support daily observation and clinician-patient communication in post-PCI management, but they should not be regarded as substitutes for clinical examinations or professional judgment. Clearer interpretive boundaries, stratified guidance, and follow-up response pathways are needed to help patients appropriately understand and act on device-generated information.

papers.title: Decoding Sleep and Cardiovascular Risk: Methodological Insights and Bridging Culture Factors.
"A Father and Daughter Presentation of Autosomal Dominant Sleep-Related Hypermotor Epilepsy Via a DEPDC5 Deletion in Exon 28".
papers.abstract: Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) is a form of focal epilepsy that can be caused by a pathogenic autosomal-dominant DEP domain containing Protein 5 (DEPDC5) variant. Given its variable clinical presentation and etiology, SHE can be challenging to diagnose and treat effectively. This case describes a father-daughter pair who experienced sleep-related seizures with similar semiologies and were later diagnosed with autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (ADSHE) after genetic test results revealed that they each had a DEPDC5 deletion in Exon 28. Currently, seizures are well controlled in the father with lacosamide plus brivaracetam and in the daughter with lacosamide alone. Due to the technically difficult nature inherent in diagnosing ADSHE, both father and daughter experienced diagnostic and treatment delays. This case report highlights the importance of early pattern recognition and genetic testing in patients with clinical features of ADSHE and expands upon the current understanding of clinical presentations of pathogenic DEPDC5 variants.

papers.title: Repeated prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation improves behavioral regulation and modulates resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with problematic smartphone use: a randomized sham-controlled longitudinal study.
papers.abstract: Problematic smartphone use (PSU) has emerged as an increasingly prevalent digital behavioral addiction among young adults and is associated with impaired executive control, excessive craving, and altered large-scale brain network organization. Although transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has demonstrated therapeutic potential for addictive disorders, its neurophysiological mechanisms in PSU remain insufficiently understood. This study investigated whether repeated prefrontal tDCS improves behavioral outcomes and reorganizes resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. Eighty participants meeting validated criteria for PSU were randomly assigned to receive active (n = 40) or sham (n = 40) tDCS. Active stimulation (2.0 mA, 20 min/session, three sessions/week for 12 weeks) targeted the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Behavioral outcomes included objectively recorded smartphone use, Smartphone Addiction Scale-Short Version scores, ecological momentary assessment craving, and work and social functioning. Resting-state EEG was recorded under eyes-closed and eyes-open conditions before and after intervention. Canonical EEG microstate temporal characteristics were analyzed using mixed repeated-measures analysis with false discovery rate correction. Compared with sham stimulation, active tDCS significantly reduced objectively measured smartphone use, craving intensity, and functional impairment while improving behavioral regulation. Neurophysiologically, active stimulation selectively reorganized resting-state brain dynamics. During eyes-closed recording, microstate C occurrence decreased whereas microstate D occurrence increased significantly. During eyes-open recording, both the occurrence and coverage of microstate B increased following active stimulation. No significant changes were observed in global explained variance, suggesting that repeated tDCS primarily modified the temporal organization rather than the spatial configuration of resting-state brain activity. Repeated prefrontal tDCS produced concurrent behavioral improvement and selective reorganization of resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. These findings provide preliminary evidence that repeated prefrontal tDCS is associated with concurrent behavioral changes and alterations in resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. Further confirmatory studies are needed to determine the clinical and mechanistic significance of these neurophysiological changes.

papers.title: Machine learning-assisted chemometric analysis of salivary ATR-FTIR spectra for the diagnosis of oral submucous fibrosis.
papers.abstract: Oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF) is a chronic, potentially malignant disorder strongly linked to areca nut chewing. Clinical diagnosis is challenging, and histopathology, though the gold standard, is invasive and subject to inter-observer variability. Saliva analysis using Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy offers a promising non-invasive alternative. This study evaluated salivary ATR-FTIR spectral analysis integrated with machine learning for classification of OSMF, individuals with adverse oral habits, and healthy controls. Unstimulated saliva samples were collected from 450 participants comprising 150 patients with clinically diagnosed OSMF, 150 individuals with adverse oral habits without clinical evidence of OSMF, and 150 healthy controls. After centrifugation, the saliva supernatant was analyzed by ATR-FTIR spectroscopy over 400-4000 cm-¹. Spectra underwent baseline correction and normalization followed by Savitzky-Golay smoothing. For machine-learning analysis, Standard Scaler and PCA were incorporated within the classification pipeline. Decision Tree, Random Forest, support vector machine (SVM), and XGBoost classifiers were evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. Hyperparameter optimization and performance estimation used the same cross-validation framework. An independent cohort of 90 participants was used for validation. XGBoost showed the highest cross-validation performance, with accuracies of 90.62% for Normal versus Habit, 97.67% for Normal versus OSMF, and 91.30% for three-class classification. Statistical analysis identified 157 nominally significant wavenumbers (p<0.05) within a continuous region from 1581 to 2142 cm-¹ corresponding to protein and collagen bands. Principal component analysis showed that PC1 and PC2 explained 89.26% and 6.95% of the total variance, respectively (96.21% cumulatively). In the independent validation cohort, accuracy was 80.0% for OSMF versus Normal and 71.7% for Habit versus Normal. Salivary ATR-FTIR combined with machine learning demonstrated promising classification performance and preliminary performance in an independent cohort. The identified spectral region is biologically plausible in the context of altered salivary biochemical composition associated with inflammation and fibrosis, but it should not be regarded as a validated disease-specific biomarker. Salivary ATR-FTIR is best considered a complementary, non-invasive screening and risk-stratification approach rather than a replacement for clinical/oral examination or histopathological assessment when biopsy is indicated. Larger, diverse, multicenter studies with rigorous validation are needed before clinical implementation.

papers.title: In-person UCLA-PEERS® program for adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in Italy: study protocol for a pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial with pragmatic features and exploratory EEG markers of treatment response.
papers.abstract: Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Level 1 frequently experience persistent difficulties in peer relationships and social functioning that become more evident as social demands increase. Group-based social skills trainings represent a key evidence-based intervention for this population, yet its availability in routine clinical services is still limited. The Program for the Education and Enrichment of Relational Skills (PEERS®) is one of the most empirically supported interventions for autistic adolescents. In Italy, telemedicine delivery has shown promising results, but the effectiveness and implementation of the in-person format in real-world services have not yet been evaluated. In addition, predictors of individual response to psychosocial interventions remain largely unknown. This study is designed as a two-arm pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial incorporating pragmatic features, including delivery within a routine tertiary clinical service, comparison with Treatment as Usual (TAU), and allowance for ongoing concomitant clinical, educational, and pharmacological treatments. It will compare the in-person Italian adaptation of UCLA PEERS® with Treatment as Usual (TAU) at IRCCS Fondazione Stella Maris (Pisa, Italy). Thirty-six adolescents aged 11-13 years with ASD (DSM-5-TR) and Full-Scale IQ >85 will be assessed at baseline (T0) and after the 16-week intervention (T1). Randomization will use block allocation with allocation concealment until completion of baseline assessments; outcome assessors and independent ADOS-BOSCC video coders will remain blind to group assignment. The intervention includes sixteen weekly 90-minute group sessions delivered by certified providers, with parallel caregiver sessions and structured teacher contacts to promote generalization. The primary focus of this pilot trial is feasibility, assessed through recruitment, retention, session attendance, and treatment fidelity. Clinical outcomes will be examined exploratorily to provide preliminary estimates of treatment effects. The QSQ-R will serve as the prespecified principal clinical outcome for estimating change in social functioning from baseline to T1. Parent- and adolescent-report versions will be analyzed separately, considering the Social Initiative and Social Reciprocity dimensions as distinct outcomes rather than deriving a composite total score. Key secondary outcomes include social knowledge (TASSK-R), autism-related social responsiveness (SRS-2), social motivation (SSDS), social anxiety (SAS), and observational change in social-communication behaviors (ADOS-BOSCC). Emotional-behavioral functioning (CBCL; YSR) will be explored as additional secondary outcomes. Baseline electroencephalography (EEG) recorded during a gesture-word integration task will be used to derive the N400 congruency effect and to explore whether individual differences in this measure are associated with treatment response. As a pilot and feasibility trial, the study is not powered for definitive efficacy testing and will estimate feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and preliminary effect sizes to inform future multicenter trials. This study will provide the first evaluation of in-person PEERS® in the Italian clinical context and test the generalizability of previous telemedicine findings in routine care. The integration of clinical and behavioral outcomes may contribute to mechanism-informed, personalized psychosocial interventions for autistic adolescents and guide the design of future confirmatory studies. (ClinicalTrials.gov - NCT07207213 - October, 3, 2025).

papers.title: Correlation between phenotype and polysomnography findings of sleep-disordered breathing in term, non-syndromic infants: a case series study.
papers.abstract: Sleep-disordered breathing (SBD) is understudied in non-syndromic term infants since most of the research focuses on high-risk groups such as premature infants or those with underlying medical conditions. There is a gap in our understanding of phenotypes that predispose this population to experience SDB. Threshold for diagnosis remain poorly standardized, and there is limited data on effective treatment strategies. To characterize the clinical presentation and polysomnographic features of term, non-syndromic, infants referred for evaluation of suspected sleep-disordered breathing (SDB). This was a single-center case series of review of polysomnographic (PSG) data in non-syndromic term infants from 0-12 months of age from a tertiary care center. Fifteen infants met inclusion criteria. The mean gestational age was 38.4 ± 0.6 weeks; 80% were male. The mean age at initial PSG was 7.5 ± 3.6 months. Snoring was present in 33% and 47% carried a diagnosis of gastroesophageal reflux (GER). The average apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was 23.1/h. The mean obstructive AHI (OAHI) was 20/h and the mean central apnea index (CAI) was 3.1/h. Mean oxygen saturation was 97.5 ± 1.5%, with a nadir of 81.0 ± 9.9%. Six patients met criteria for sleep-related hypoxemia (SpO2 < 90% for ≥ 5 min). Mean and peak CO2 levels were 35 mmHg and 48.6 mmHg, respectively. None of the patients met criteria for sleep-related hypoventilation (CO2 > 50 mmHg for > 25% of total sleep time). 71% of the infants underwent an evaluation of their upper airway, and 7 had abnormal findings. Follow-up PSG obtained around 13.4 months, on average, in 10 of the infants showed resolution of SDB in 4 infants. One patient showed resolution of the SDB with CPAP, but was lost to follow-up. SDB was persistent but improved in 5 infants. AHI showed a weak negative correlation with age (ρ = -0.31, p = 0.26). Frequency of moderate-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is high among non-syndromic term infants. The clinical implication of this is still unclear. However, AHI does appear to decrease with age, and many infants are able to outgrow their OSA without any intervention. Further research is warranted to refine diagnostic thresholds and standardize the diagnostic evaluation and interventions for SDB in this unique population.

papers.title: Three-year trajectories of insomnia symptoms among young breast cancer survivors.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruptions are common in cancer survivors and can negatively impact quality of life. Young breast cancer survivors face unique challenges and may have distinct sleep patterns. We examined trajectories of insomnia symptoms over 3 years among young survivors. 836 women, ≤45 years old with stage I-III breast cancer, were recruited to the Menstrual Cycle Maintenance and Quality of Life After Breast Cancer Study within 8 months of diagnosis. Insomnia symptoms were assessed at 6-month intervals from baseline through 3 years post-recruitment, using the Women's Health Initiative Insomnia Rating Scale (WHIIRS). Group-based trajectory modeling was used to identify distinct trajectories of insomnia symptoms. The final model was chosen by comparing the average posterior probability of assignment (PPA) and examining the distinctiveness and interpretability of the trajectories. Key demographic, quality of life and clinical variables were assessed in multinomial logistic regression models as potential factors associated with group membership. The mean age of participants was 38 years (range: 20-45 years) at enrollment. Three distinct insomnia trajectories were identified: low probability of insomnia (n=277, 33.1%), moderate probability (n=354, 42.4%), and high probability (n=205, 24.5%). Average PPA was between 75%-82% for each group. Insomnia symptoms were highest at baseline but improved for the low probability and moderate probability groups. In adjusted models, older age (p=0.02), lower education (p=0.03), having received chemotherapy (p=0.03), night sweats (p=0.02), lower SF-12 physical component scores (poorer physical functioning, p<0.0001), and lower SF-12 mental health component scores (p<0.0001) were associated with participants in the moderate and high probability insomnia groups compared to those in the low probability group. Insomnia symptoms are problematic for many young breast cancer survivors. Future studies are needed to determine whether early identification and intervention can modify these insomnia symptom trajectories and improve broader survivorship outcomes.

papers.title: Plant-derived nutrition and perimenopausal emotional health: current evidence and research priorities.
papers.abstract: Perimenopause combines ovarian hormone variability with changes in stress regulation, inflammatory-redox balance, neuroplasticity, and gut-brain metabolism, creating a period of increased vulnerability to depressive symptoms, anxiety, irritability, and sleep disturbance. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on plant-derived foods, bioactives, dietary supplements, and standardized botanical preparations relevant to emotional health during the menopausal transition. Targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus identified literature published through 31 July 2026. Evidence was classified by consumed form and reproductive-stage directness and integrated across three regulatory axes: endocrine-stress regulation, immune-redox-neuroplasticity, and gut-brain-metabolic communication. Human evidence includes small randomized trials of standardized saffron, rhapontic rhubarb, fenugreek, ashwagandha, and shatavari preparations, with product-specific psychological-symptom signals, as well as a null Hypericum-Vitex trial. Evidence for plant-rich dietary patterns and isolated bioactives derives mainly from broader menopausal or adult populations. Across studies, reproductive stage, exposure composition, symptom endpoint, and preparation standardization emerge as key determinants of interpretation. Linking symptom clusters with proposed pathway involvement generates hypotheses for prospective phenotype-stratified nutrition trials. Future studies should combine reproductive staging using the Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop + 10 (STRAW+10) framework, prespecified emotional outcomes, dietary assessment, standardized product characterization, exposure biomarkers, metabotype profiling, and safety monitoring. This framework positions plant-derived nutrition as a testable component of perimenopausal emotional-health research and functional-food development.

papers.title: Case Report: Successful treatment of drug-resistant epilepsy with unilateral deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT-DBS) is an established palliative treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) and is conventionally performed bilaterally. However, the efficacy of unilateral ANT-DBS remains unclear. We report a patient with DRE who underwent unilateral ANT-DBS because of an epileptogenic network predominantly involving one side and anatomical constraints precluding electrode implantation on the contralateral side. A 29-year-old female underwent comprehensive presurgical evaluation, including seizure semiology assessment, video-electroencephalography (EEG), computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging. She developed DRE following multimodal treatment for a suprasellar germ cell tumor during childhood. Despite multiple antiseizure medications and vagus nerve stimulation, she continued to experience approximately 10 habitual seizures per day. Seizure semiology was characterized by asymmetric tonic posturing of the limbs lasting 10-30 s, followed by an atonic phase. EEG findings indicated a widespread epileptogenic network predominantly involving the right frontal and temporal areas. Brain imaging showed severe left hemispheric atrophy, marked widening of the left subdural space, and a pre-existing shunt system, which prevented identification of the left ANT. Therefore, DBS implantation was performed in the right ANT alone. Stimulation was initiated 7 days after surgery at an intensity of 2 mA. Following initiation of right ANT stimulation, seizure frequency decreased from approximately 10 to one per day, likely due to a microlesioning effect. Thereafter, right ANT stimulation was associated with a sustained seizure reduction of approximately 60%. Postoperative EEG demonstrated a reduction in interictal epileptiform discharges. The clinical benefit was maintained at the 9-month follow-up, with no surgery- or stimulation-related adverse events were observed. Unilateral ANT-DBS can provide clinically meaningful seizure control in carefully selected patients whose predominant epileptogenic network is localized to one cerebral hemisphere. This approach may represent a feasible therapeutic option when anatomical or surgical constraints prevent conventional bilateral ANT electrode implantation. Further studies with larger patient cohorts and longer follow-up periods are required to clarify the indications, durability, and efficacy of unilateral ANT-DBS.

papers.title: NPAS2 attenuates diabetic cardiomyopathy by preserving pyruvate dehydrogenase activity and mitochondrial metabolic homeostasis.
papers.abstract: Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a serious cardiac complication of diabetes, characterized by myocardial metabolic dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and structural remodeling. Disruption of circadian clock genes has been implicated in metabolic diseases, yet the role of neuronal PAS domain protein 2 (NPAS2), a core circadian regulator, in DCM remains poorly understood. NPAS2 expression and circadian rhythmicity were assessed in the myocardium of T2DM and db/db mice. Cardiac-specific Npas2 knockout (Npas2 cko) mice were subjected to high-fat diet combined with streptozotocin (HFD + STZ) to model DCM and evaluate cardiac function, remodeling, and metabolic profiles. H9c2 cardiomyocytes were used for loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments under high glucose/high fat (HGHF) conditions, and rescue experiments targeting pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) were performed to establish downstream mechanisms. Finally, adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (AAV9) mediated NPAS2 overexpression was delivered in vivo to evaluate its therapeutic potential. Myocardial NPAS2 expression was significantly reduced and its circadian oscillations were disrupted in diabetic mice. Cardiomyocyte-specific Npas2 deletion exacerbated HFD + STZ-induced cardiac dysfunction, hypertrophy, fibrosis, and lipid accumulation. In H9c2 cells, NPAS2 knockdown impaired mitochondrial respiration, increased apoptosis, elevated triglyceride and free fatty acid contents, and reduced PDH activity. Conversely, NPAS2 overexpression reversed these detrimental effects under HGHF conditions. Rescue experiments demonstrated that PDH overexpression mitigated the damage caused by NPAS2 knockdown, whereas PDH silencing abolished the protective effects of NPAS2 overexpression. In vivo, AAV9-mediated NPAS2 overexpression significantly improved cardiac function, attenuated hypertrophy and fibrosis, and restored lipid and glucose homeostasis in diabetic WT and Npas2 cko mice. NPAS2 protects the heart against diabetic cardiomyopathy by maintaining PDH-dependent mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and metabolic homeostasis, representing a promising therapeutic target for DCM.

papers.title: Rivastigmine and Emerging Nanotechnological Strategies for Targeted Delivery: A Comprehensive Review.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease affects millions of people globally; it is an irreversible and incurable disease, characterized by gradual cognitive decline as well as pathophysiological changes including the presence of senile plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. There are several risk factors associated with Alzheimer's disease, including elevated blood pressure, blood sugar concentration, alcohol consumption, smoking, and sleep disturbances. Rivastigmine is an FDA-approved cholinesterase inhibitor used to treat Alzheimer's disease. It is available as oral solutions, capsules, and transdermal patches. Oral administration can lead to detrimental and off-target effects such as nausea and vomiting, and the use of patches can cause irritation and rashes. Across various systems, including the Cardiovascular (CVS), Gastrointestinal (GI), immunological, dermatological, and respiratory systems, rivastigmine has been associated with effects that further necessitate targeted drug delivery. Novel drug delivery systems such as Liposomes, Polymeric Nanoparticles, Dendrimers, Solid Lipid Nanoparticles (SLNs), Nanostructured Lipid Carriers (NLCs), nano-emulsions, and Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles (MSNs) have been developed to address the limitations of conventional dosage forms. These new formulations possess the ability to increase drug loading capacity, enhance penetration across the BBB, reduce expulsion, and offer controlled release of the drug. As a result, rivastigmine can be targeted to the intended site, with fewer off-target effects. However, formulation-specific toxicity may still occur. Positive off-target effects, such as improved appetite, protection against malnutrition, and evidence of advantage in treating colitis, were also observed with rivastigmine. However, detailed studies of its mechanism of action are needed to provide a scientifically sound justification for repurposing rivastigmine. Google Scholar and PubMed were searched for literature for this review and included studies that met the criteria.

papers.title: Pharmacokinetics, Metabolism, Disposition, and Neuropharmacological Mechanisms of Jujuboside A: A Review.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a frequently occurring sleep disorder that is associated with a reduced quality of life and a higher risk of neuropsychological, metabolic, and inflammatory diseases. Jujuboside A (JuA), a dammarane-type triterpenoid saponin obtained from Ziziphi Spinosae Semen (Suanzaoren), has shown promise as a therapeutic agent for insomnia. The present review summarizes the available evidence re-garding the pharmacokinetics, metabolism, disposition, sedative-hypnotic activity, and neuroprotective effects of JuA. It is believed that JuA acts as a multi-target agent for both the treatment of insomnia and for providing neuroprotection, even though it has a low oral bioavailability (about 1.32%) and limited ability to penetrate the brain (with a brain-to-plasma ratio of 0.1-0.3). JuA is subject to extensive metab-olism in the intestine and liver, this being performed via the body's glycosidases and by the gut microbi-ota, and is eliminated via both the biliary and renal routes. The drug seems to influence sleep mainly through GABAergic signaling in the Paraventricular Thalamic Nucleus (PVT), and also impacts the monoaminergic and adenosinergic pathways, the circadian rhythm, mitochondrial function in prefrontal neurons, and gut-brain interactions. The neuroprotective effects involve various pathways including Shh/Gli1/Gli2, P2X7R-BDNF, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, MAPK/ERK, Wnt/β-catenin, and YY1-mediated tran-scriptional regulation. Although the existing evidence points to the therapeutic potential of JuA, more research is still required in order to better understand its pharmacological properties and mechanisms of action. This review aims to outline the pharmacological properties and molecular features of JuA, point out the current research gaps, and suggest possible avenues for the development of therapies based on JuA.

papers.title: [Levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone combination in chronotherapy of Parkinson's disease].
papers.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy of the levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone combination in the chronotherapy of Parkinson's disease (PD). This multicenter study was conducted at seven clinical sites, with 72 patients completing the follow-up period. The efficacy of levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone administration was evaluated in relation to the daily activity profile of levodopa. Patients recorded hourly assessments of «on», «off», and dyskinesia periods in a diary before and after therapy adjustment. The follow-up period lasted one month. Patients misidentified «on» periods in 46% of cases and «off» periods in 35% of cases. The daily profile of levodopa efficacy was heterogeneous: the favorable period occurred in the morning for 40% of patients, in the afternoon for 32%, in the evening for 21%, and in the late evening for 7%. Tailoring levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone administration to the circadian profile improved outcomes in 72% of patients. A morning peak in efficacy predicted high drug sensitivity, while shifting the favorable period to the evening was associated with lower therapy efficacy. Optimizing the timing of antiparkinsonian drug administration in accordance with the circadian rhythm of PD symptoms may enhance therapeutic efficacy. Chronotherapy that incorporates the circadian profile of levodopa efficacy can maximize the benefits of levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone combination therapy.

papers.title: [Phenotype-driven approach for safinamide use in Parkinson's disease].
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is now recognized as a multisystem neurodegenerative disorder marked by the progressive disintegration of large-scale functional networks in the brain, a phenomenon termed connectomopathy. The clinical heterogeneity of PD reflects the distinct patterns of neuronal ensemble involvement in individual patients, contributing to both motor and non-motor symptoms. This perspective highlights the necessity of a phenotype-driven approach when selecting anti-Parkinsonian therapies. This article examines the role of safinamide, a drug with dual mechanisms of action: reversible inhibition of monoamine oxidase-B and anti-glutamatergic properties, within the framework of personalized PD management. Clinical case analyses demonstrate that safinamide prolongs the «on» period without a significant increase in dyskinesias and provides additional therapeutic benefits for non-motor symptoms, including chronic pain, depression, and sleep disturbances.

papers.title: [Anhedonia in Parkinson's disease: findings from the first national clinical and statistical study of motor and non-motor associations].
papers.abstract: To evaluate anhedonia severity in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) and examine its associations with demographic, motor, and non-motor characteristics. The study included 390 patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. Participants were classified into two groups by anhedonia severity: without anhedonia (<3 points; 77 patients, 19.7%) and with anhedonia (≥3 points; 313 patients, 80.3%). All participants underwent comprehensive clinical and neurological evaluations. The variables analyzed included age, age at PD onset, disease duration, Hoehn and Yahr stage, rate of progression, presence of dyskinesias, Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) scores I-III, total UPDRS score, Schwab-England scale, anxiety, depression, cognitive status, sleep quality, apathy, and asthenia. Statistical analyses included the Mann-Whitney test, Spearman's correlation analysis, and multivariate linear regression with robust standard errors. The cohort's median anhedonia score was 4.0 [3.0; 6.0] points. Statistically significant correlations were identified between anhedonia and depressive symptoms (ρ=0.668; p<0.001; q<0.001), anxiety (ρ=0.277; p<0.001; q=0.001), Hoehn and Yahr stage (ρ=0.208; p<0.001; q<0.001), patient age (ρ=0.187; p<0.001; q=0.001), age at disease onset (ρ=0.145; p=0.006; q=0.025), and cognitive status (ρ=-0.199; p=0.009; q=0.028). Comparative analysis showed that patients with anhedonia had higher depression scores (9.0 [7.0; 11.0] versus 5.0 [4.0; 7.0] points; p<0.001; q<0.001), were older (68.0 [63.0; 74.0] versus 65.0 [58.0; 71.0] years; p=0.003; q=0.020), had lower cognitive status scores (23.0 [20.0; 25.0] versus 25.0 [24.0; 27.0] points; p=0.009; q=0.042), and lower sleep quality scores (12.0 [6.0; 18.0] versus 18.0 [14.8; 22.2] points; p=0.002; q=0.020). In the multivariate regression model, depressive symptoms were the only independent predictor of anhedonia severity (β=0.509; 95% CI 0.329 to 0.689; p<0.001; q<0.001). Anhedonia is a prevalent non-motor manifestation of PD, identified in most patients in this cohort. It is most strongly associated with depressive symptoms, which remain independently significant in multivariate analysis. Anhedonia is not directly related to motor severity, disease duration, dyskinesias, or functional independence. These results suggest that anhedonia is primarily an affective non-motor component of PD and should be specifically assessed in clinical practice.

papers.title: [Multimodal biomarkers of Parkinson's disease risk in essential tremor. (A prospective cohort study)].
papers.abstract: To identify clinical and neuroimaging biomarkers associated with Parkinson's disease (PD) onset in patients with essential tremor plus (ET-plus) during prospective observation. This prospective observational cohort study included 159 patients diagnosed with essential tremor (ET), ET-plus, ET-PD, and idiopathic PD. The median observation period was 4.6 years. All participants underwent standardized neurological examinations and assessments, including the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part III (UPDRS-III), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA), Unified Dystonia Rating Scale (UDRS), Fahn-Tolosa-Marin Tremor Rating Scale, Non-Motor Symptoms Scale (NMSS), olfactory testing, screening for probable REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), Stroop test, forward and backward counting tests, Boston Naming Test, literal and semantic verbal fluency tests, transcranial sonography (TCS) of the substantia nigra, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with nigrosome-1 assessment. Conversion from ET-plus to PD occurred in 15 patients. The most significant predictors of conversion were hyperechogenicity of the substantia nigra on transcranial Doppler (TCD), absence of nigrosome-1 on MRI, probable REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and ET duration greater than 20 years. The predictive model demonstrated high discriminatory power (C-statistic 0.89). Clinically, patients who converted showed a combination of non-motor symptoms, cognitive decline, signs of nigrostriatal dysfunction, and more frequent resting tremor. The risk of Parkinson's disease onset in patients with ET-plus is determined by a combination of multimodal biomarkers. The prospective identification of 15 patients who converted supports classifying this subgroup as a high-risk phenotype that warrants ongoing monitoring and comprehensive evaluation.

papers.title: Sleep Homeostasis Has Circaseptan and Circatrigintan Cycles Over Year-Long Timescales.
papers.abstract: Sleep homeostasis, the process by which sleep pressure accumulated during wakefulness is dissipated across non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, can be quantified as the nightly rate of decline in slow-wave activity (SWA; 0.5-4 Hz). Disruption of this homeostatic process has been documented in a range of neurological disorders including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease and REM sleep behaviour disorder, yet its long-term dynamics in healthy individuals remain uncharacterized. The advent of subscalp EEG (sqEEG) platforms now makes continuous, naturalistic sleep recording feasible over months, enabling longitudinal study of sleep homeostasis at an unprecedented scale. Here we report the first such characterization in 20 healthy adults recorded continuously over 12-15 months. SWA slope was predominantly negative across all subjects, confirming intact homeostatic regulation and was stable across sex and age. Continuous wavelet transform analysis revealed significant circaseptan (~7-day) and circatrigintan (~28-day) rhythmicity in the majority of subjects, independent of sex. These findings establish a normative baseline for long-term sleep homeostatic dynamics and suggest that homeostatic sleep pressure dissipation is organized across multiple timescales beyond the single night, with direct relevance for neurological conditions in which this process is disrupted.

papers.title: Disentangling the Genetic Relationship Between Sleep and Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: A bidirectional relationship between sleep and epilepsy is well recognised, yet the biological mechanisms linking them remain poorly understood. Both have a genetic basis, with genome-wide association studies (GWAS) capturing polygenic contributions. By leveraging GWAS summary statistics, we aimed to investigate their shared genetic architecture. We analysed seven sleep traits (morningness chronotype, sleep duration, habitual short/long sleep, insomnia, daytime napping/sleepiness) with common epilepsy types (focal epilepsy and genetic generalised epilepsy [GGE]). For each trait pair, we estimated genome-wide genetic correlation, tested bidirectional causality, quantified polygenic overlap, performed gene-trait associations to identify putative pleiotropic genes, estimated local genetic correlations and investigated whether regions of significance were driven by shared causal variants using colocalisation and fine-mapping. Genome-wide analyses supported a positive genetic correlation between higher GGE risk and habitual short sleep, with extensive polygenic overlap (75%-97%) across seven sleep traits. Gene-trait analyses identified RMI1 as a putative sleep-epilepsy candidate, with 13 additional sleep-associated genes linked to monogenic epilepsies (e.g., KANSL1, GRIN2A). Locus-specific analyses identified 16 genomic loci of interest (13 sleep-GGE, 3 sleep-focal epilepsy). Morningness-GGE shared the largest number of locus-specific associations. No significant causal relationships were identified, and causal variants did not colocalise. Our findings support complex shared genetic contributions between sleep and epilepsy, with distinct patterns for focal compared to generalised epilepsy. These differences may help explain syndrome-specific sleep-wake associations, including seizure timing and predisposition. By localising shared loci and highlighting specific overlapping genes, we provide a foundation for future research into the mechanisms underlying epilepsy-sleep comorbidities.

papers.title: [Application of orthognathic surgery in the treatment of severe adult obstructive sleep apnea].
papers.abstract: Orthognathic surgery is one of the most effective surgical techniques for the treatment of severe obstructive sleep apnea （OSA） in adults, and its application is becoming increasingly widespread. The application of strategies and techniques such as the surgery-first approach, segmental osteotomy, and counterclockwise rotation of the jaws can maximize the therapeutic potential of orthognathic surgery for severe OSA in adults. This paper reviews the indications, key surgical considerations, limitations, and future perspectives of orthognathic surgery in the treatment of OSA in adults, aiming to provide guidance for clinical practice of orthognathic surgery for severe OSA in adults.

papers.title: [Neurostimulation therapy for obstructive sleep apnea].
papers.abstract: Continuous positive airway pressure （CPAP）, the first-line therapy for obstructive sleep apnea （OSA）, is frequently limited by inadequate adherence. Neurostimulation techniques, especially hypoglossal nerve stimulation （HNS）, offer effective alternative therapeutic options for these patients. Based on the latest evidance, this review systematically delineates the current landscape and research advances in neurostimulation therapy for OSA across four dimensions: anatomical and physiological foundations, clinical implementation and efficacy stratification, risk mitigation, and future directions. Despite challenges related to cost-effectiveness, accessibility is progressively improving through surgical standardization, programming optimization, and domestic technological development. Future development of this field will involve precision phenotyping, intelligent device integration, and systematic care pathways, thereby facilitating personalized therapeutic protocols for expanded clinical populations.

papers.title: [Progress in research on olfactory dysfunction in patients with obstructive sleep apnea].
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea （OSA） is a common sleep-related breathing disorder characterized by recurrent upper-airway collapse and intermittent hypoxia, which has been widely recognized for its detrimental effects on neurocognitive function and multiple physiological systems. Emerging evidence indicates that olfactory dysfunction （OD） may represent an important yet long-overlooked manifestation in patients with OSA. Numerous clinical studies have demonstrated that olfactory threshold, discrimination, and identification abilities are significantly impaired in individuals with OSA compared with healthy controls, and the severity of olfactory deficits shows a clear negative correlation with the apnea-hypopnea index. The underlying mechanisms appear to be multifactorial:①damage to the cholinergic neurotransmitter system and cognitive impairment induced by intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation;②structural and functional alterations in brain regions involved in olfactory processing, including the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus;③the impact of elevated body mass index and chronic inflammatory responses on the olfactory epithelium and central olfactory pathways. Continuous positive airway pressure （CPAP）, the first-line therapy for OSA, may partially improve olfactory performance by enhancing ventilation, reducing hypoxemia, and alleviating airway inflammation, although current evidence remains limited by sample size and follow-up duration. Beyond standard OSA management, olfactory training, neurophysiological assessment, and inflammation-modulating interventions may serve as promising future strategies. In summary, OD is highly prevalent and clinically significant in OSA patients, with a complex pathophysiological basis involving multiple interacting factors. Larger-sample, mechanism-driven, and intervention-focused studies are warranted to deepen our understanding of OSA-related OD and to support the development of more precise therapeutic approaches.

papers.title: [Progress in titration of mandibular advancement devices in primary snoring and OSA].
papers.abstract: Oral appliances are an important alternative to continuous positive airway pressure （CPAP） for treating primarysnoring and obstructive sleep apnea （OSA）, among which customized, adjustable mandibular advancement devices （MADs） are the most widely used. Titration involves stepwise adjustment of mandibular protrusion and, when necessary, vertical opening, to identify an individualized therapeutic window and the minimum effective protrusion that balance efficacy and tolerability. This article reviews advances in MAD titration techniques from 2021 to 2025, including conventional subjective stepwise titration, polysomnography-guided or remotely controlled mandibular positioning, drug-induced sleep endoscopyguided titration, home signal-driven objective titration, and automated or position-responsive devices. The indications,advantages, and limitations of each approach are critically evaluated. Overall, objective and remotely guided closed-loop titration may shorten the time to therapeutic optimization and reduce clinic visits. However, study heterogeneity and limitedlong-term follow-up highlight the need for standardized reporting and long-term real-world validation.

papers.title: [Research on obstructive sleep apnea and sleep bruxism].
papers.abstract: Objective:The aim of this study was to explore the potential causal relationship between obstructive sleep apnea（OSA） and sleep bruxism（SB） through Mendelian randomization（MR） analysis, a method widely used in genetic research. Methods:We extracted genetic instrumental variables for OSA from the publicly available GWAS catalog database and for SB from the FinnGen database. We designed bidirectional two-sample MR analyses to comprehensively assess the genetic association of OSA with SB. We performed MR analyses using inverse variance weighting（IVW）, weighted median, MR-Egger, Simple Mode, and Weighted Mode, as well as sensitivity analyses to assess whether the results were robust. Results:OSA had no significant effect on SB（OR=1.71, 95%CI 0.67-4.32, P＝0.26>0.05）, reverse MR analysis similarly failed to find a significant association between SB and OSA（OR=1.01, 95%CI 0.99-1.03, P＝0.39>0.05）. Conclusion:This MR analysis found no genetic evidence of bidirectional causality between OSA and SB, and the results of this study do not support the existence of a direct, reciprocal pathogenic effect between OSA and SB.

papers.title: [A multi-cohort clinical study of magnesium metabolism dysregulation in patients with obstructive sleep apnea].
papers.abstract: Objective:Based on multi-cohort clinical data, this study systematically investigated the potential association between obstructive sleep apnea（OSA） and magnesium（Mg） metabolic dysregulation, aiming to provide new evidence for the early identification and intervention of OSA-related metabolic complications. Methods:First, data from 410 385 Finnish participants in the FinnGen database（43 901 OSA patients and 366 484 controls） were analyzed in conjunction with genetic variation data for seven trace elements from genome-wide association studies（GWAS）. Multi-method Mendelian randomization analyses were conducted to assess the causal relationship between OSA and Mg levels. Subsequently, 199 Chinese Han participants from the Sleep Monitoring Center of Qilu Hospital, Shandong University, were enrolled, with measurements of serum Mg and various biochemical indicators. Multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed based on OSA severity and serum Mg levels to validate findings. Results:In the Finnish cohort, body Mg levels were significantly inversely associated with OSA risk（P=0.017, OR<1）, indicating lower Mg status in OSA patients. In the Chinese Han cohort, the proportions of alcohol consumption, blood urea, serum creatinine, and serum Mg progressively increased across controls, mild-to-moderate OSA, and severe OSA groups（P<0.05）, whereas eGFR and oxygen saturation progressively decreased（P<0.05）. Multivariate ordinal logistic regression identified serum Mg as an independent risk factor for OSA（OR>1, P<0.05）. Further stratification by serum Mg revealed that the high-Mg group had a higher apnea-hypopnea index（AHI）, more severe renal impairment, and lower eGFR（all P<0.05）, with multivariate analysis confirming AHI as an independent risk factor for elevated serum Mg（OR>1, P<0.05）. Conclusion:This study may demonstrate a biphasic Mg dysregulation in OSA patients, characterized by reduced tissue Mg but elevated serum Mg. Intermittent hypoxia associated with OSA may contribute to Mg depletion at the cellular and tissue levels, while concomitant renal impairment may reduce renal Mg excretion, resulting in elevated serum Mg despite underlying tissue Mg deficiency. These findings suggest that Mg metabolic dysregulation may serve as a key pathological feature of OSA, providing a novel perspective for stratified management.

papers.title: [Clinical evaluation of maxillomandibular advancement in the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea].
papers.abstract: Objective:To analyze the treatment efficacy of maxillomandibular advancement（MMA） in obstructive sleep apnea（OSA）. Methods:Twenty-two patients with moderate to severe OSA admitted to Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital from June 2021 to September 2025 were enrolled. All patients exhibited CPAP intolerance or poor treatment response, and drug-induced sleep endoscopy revealed centripetal collapse of the velopharynx and lateral pharyngeal wall collapse. All patients underwent MMA. The body mass index（BMI）, epworth sleepiness scale（ESS） score, polysomnography（PSG） index, and clinical efficacy were collected preoperatively and at 6 months postoperatively. Results:At 6 months postoperatively, among the 22 patients, 3 patients achieved cure（13.64%）, 10 were markedly effective（45.45%）, 6 were effective（27.27%） and 3 were ineffective（13.64%）, yielding an overall clinical effective rate of 86.36%. Compared with preoperative values, postoperative AHI decreased, LSaO2 increased, and ESS score were reduced（P<0.05）; no significant difference was found in BMI between preoperative and postoperative measurements（P>0.05）. Conclusion:MMA can effectively increase the upper airway volume, reduce the frequency of apnea-hypopnea, and improve nocturnal hypoxemia and daytime sleepiness in patients with OSA. For patients with moderate to severe OSA who are intolerant to CPAP and present with concurrent palatopharyngeal and lateral pharyngeal collapse, MMA serves as an effective treatment option.

papers.title: [Evaluation of airway obstruction and surgical outcomes in OSA patients with small tonsils through drug-induced sleep endoscopy].
papers.abstract: Objective:To evaluate the upper airway obstruction patterns in obstructive sleep apnea（OSA） patients with tonsils of grade Ⅰ°-Ⅱ° using drug-induced sleep endoscopy（DISE）, and to analyze the outcomes of DISE-guided surgery. A retrospective analysis was conducted on OSA patients with grade Ⅰ°-Ⅱ° tonsil size treated between 2017 and 2020. Obstruction characteristics were recorded according to the VOTE classification based on DISE. The characteristics of upper airway obstruction were compared across subgroups stratified by OSA severity and tongue base position（grade Ⅰ°-Ⅱ° : low-grade tongue base collapse; grade Ⅲ°-Ⅳ°: high-grade tongue base collapse）. Patients who underwent DISE-guided surgery and completed follow-up were further enrolled to assess surgical efficacy and identify factors affecting postoperative outcomes. A total of 112 patients were included in the DISE analysis, including 30 patients with low-grade tongue base collapse and 82 with high-grade tongue base collapse. Retrovelar obstruction had the highest prevalence（66.7% to 84.1%） among all obstruction sites. The proportion of oropharyngeal lateral wall collapse increased with the severity of OSA. Forty-five patients completed surgery and follow-up. Surgery was performed according to DISE-based surgical planning. The surgical success rate in the low-grade tongue base collapse group（76.9%） was higher than that in the high-grade tongue base collapse group（52.9%）, but the difference was not statistically significant（P=0.259）. Postoperative AHI and percentage of time with oxygen saturation below 90% were significantly lower in the low-grade tongue base collapse group（P<0.05）. Among patients with complete concentric collapse of the retrovelar space（CCC） or complete oropharyngeal lateral wall collapse（O）, the surgical success rate was 81.8% in the low-grade tongue base collapse group versus 50.0% in the high-grade tongue base collapse group（P=0.193）. Among 6 high-grade tongue base collapse patients presenting with isolated CCC/O who underwent velopharyngeal surgery combined with partial glossectomy, 4 were effective（66.7%）; all 3 patients who underwent velopharyngeal surgery alone were ineffective. The velopharyngeal region is the primary site of obstruction in OSA patients with grade Ⅰ°-Ⅱ° tonsils and merits careful consideration during surgical planning. Patients with a low-grade tongue base collapse achieve better responses to DISE-guided surgery. For patients with high-grade tongue base collapse and CCC/O collapse subtype, combining tongue base surgery with velopharyngeal surgery may improve surgical outcomes.

papers.title: [Modified genioglossus advancement with double trapezoidal osteotomy for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea].
papers.abstract: Objective:To explore the feasibility, safety and efficacy of modified genioglossus advancement with double trapezoidal osteotomy in the treatment of specific types of obstructive sleep apnea（OSA）. Methods:The clinical data of 28 OSA patients with Friedman type Ⅱ or Ⅲ and mandibular micrognathia admitted to Foresea Life Insurance Guangzhou General Hospital and its collaborating institutions from January 2021 to December 2024 were collected and analyzed. All patients underwent modified genioglossus advancement with double trapezoidal osteotomy, and corresponding auxiliary procedures were combined according to the obstruction level: modified uvulopalatopharyngoplasty（UPPP） was added for patients with tonsillar hypertrophy or palatopharyngeal plane stenosis, lingual tonsillectomy for those with lingual tonsillar hypertrophy, and midline glossectomy or radiofrequency ablation of the tongue for those with significant tongue hypertrophy and retraction. Preoperative three-dimensional reconstruction of maxillofacial CT combined with Mimics software was performed for surgical planning to determine the parameters of double trapezoidal osteotomy（height: 14-16 mm, upper width: 20-22 mm, lower width: 23-25 mm）. During the operation, osteotomy, advancement（about 12 mm） and "Z"-shaped titanium plate fixation were completed according to the plan. Postoperative follow-up was conducted regularly to evaluate the efficacy. Results:All 28 operations were performed uneventfully, with an operation time of（95±15） minutes and intraoperative blood loss of（50±10） mL. Postoperatively, 6 patients had mild mental swelling and ecchymosis, which subsided spontaneously 3-5 days after surgery; 3 patients had transient numbness of the lower lip（in the distribution area of the mental nerve）, and the sensation recovered within 1 month after surgery; 2 patients had mandibular midline fracture and mild loosening of bone fragments due to forceful mouth opening and teeth clenching 3 days after surgery, which healed after fixation with dental arch guide plate for 3 months by the department of stomatology without affecting the final efficacy. All patients were hospitalized for 5-7 days after surgery and discharged uneventfully, without serious complications such as massive postoperative hemorrhage, dyspnea, surgical site infection, or titanium plate loosening. At the 6-month follow-up, the average snoring VAS scores before and after surgery were 7.75±1.82 and 3.61±1.75, respectively, and the average ESS scores were 9.93±4.97 and 5.54±3.09, respectively, with statistically significant differences（P<0.05）. Comparison of polysomnography results before and after surgery showed that the average AHI was（47.87±26.33） events/h and（20.89±18.35） events/h, respectively, with a statistically significant difference（P<0.01）, and the average AHI decreased by 56.36% after surgery compared with before surgery. The lowest oxygen saturation was（72.29±12.64）% before surgery and（83.50±7.93）% after surgery, with a statistically significant difference（P<0.01）. Facial evaluation at 6 months after surgery showed that the appearance of mandibular retrognathia was significantly improved in 26 patients（76.5%）. Conclusion:Modified genioglossus advancement with double trapezoidal osteotomy, fixed by tenon-and-mortise, yields high stability and a low complication profile. It can effectively enlarge the retroglossal airway, ameliorate obstructive sleep apnea（OSA） symptoms, optimize facial contour, and improve patient satisfaction simultaneously. This procedure holds high clinical application value for patients with Friedman type Ⅱ or Ⅲ（non-very severe） OSA associated with mandibular micrognathia. For patients with severe OSA, combined multi-level surgery or noninvasive ventilation therapy is required. Rigorous patient selection and exclusion of very severe cases are the keys to ensuring the success rate of treatment.
